Hirschsprung's disease is a disorder of the large intestine (colon), in which nerve cells that normally help control muscles in the wall of the colon don't migrate during fetal development to their final position in the colon wall. This causes parts of the colon to pull together too strongly when the muscles there contract (peristalsis), which can cause severe obstruction of the flow of food through the colon. Symptoms may include swelling of the abdomen (distention) and vomiting of bile, a greenish fluid produced by the liver. Hirschsprung's disease most commonly affects newborns. Surgery can relieve symptoms and prevent complications such as inflammation of the intestines (enterocolitis). With timely treatment, outlook is usually good. Phosphofructokinase (PFK) is the key enzyme in the rate determining step of glycolysis. It catalyses the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and is controlled allosterically by its substrate (fructose-6-phosphate) and ATP. As ATP concentration increases so does PFK activity decrease. Increasing levels of ADP and AMP are also likely to reduce PFK activity as they indicate that ATP needs to be remade. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate acts as a positive effector on PFK by allosterically stimulating its activity. This molecule is made from fructose-6-phosphate by PFK itself. Fructose-6-phosphate inhibits PFK as it binds to the same site as ATP. This means that increasing levels of fructose-6-phosphate will cause a fall in PFK activity. However, it is not very effective at this as the Km (Michaelis-Menten constant) for fructose-6-phosphate is fairly low (around 0.5 mM). This means that although fructose-6-phosphate has a small effect on inhibiting PFK, it is not the main regulator. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate inhibits PFK by binding to an allosteric site and switching off the enzyme. It does not have much effect at lower levels but really starts to inhibit PFK once levels reach around 10 mM. This causes problems when cells need to take up glucose as excess fructose-1,6-bisphosphate signals to the cell that there is no need to take up more glucose. This means that if a lot of glucose is taken up, there will be a build up of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and it will start to inhibit PFK. This is one of the reasons why insulin resistance can occur. Addison's disease is a chronic endocrine disorder caused by loss of adrenal gland function (including the adrenal medulla), usually due to autoimmune adrenalitis. Primary adrenal insufficiency involves a partial or complete lack of adrenocortical hormones (glucocorticoids - such as cortisol/hydrocortisone, mineralocorticoids - such as aldosterone, and possibly androgens). This may result in low blood pressure, muscle weakness, vomiting, and fatigue. Symptoms often come on slowly over months and include weakness, feeling tired, low mood, diarrhoea, and skin discoloration. In children, frequent vomiting and dehydration are common. Complications may include adrenal crisis, high blood calcium, and low bone density. Addison's disease is generally due to an autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands. Other causes include infection, cancer, and other diseases affecting the adrenal glands. Diagnosis is based on blood test and/or stimulation tests.Blood tests typically show low sodium and high potassium.The stimulation test measures the response of cortisol to synthetic ACTH.A low dose of synthetic ACTH (cosyntropin) is injected into a vein. Spina bifida is caused by failure of closure of the neural tube during embryonic development. It results in a characteristic pattern of birth defects. These include damage to the brain, spinal cord and/or the coverings of the brain and spinal cord.  The presence of a tuft of hair (also known as a "chiari malformation") can be seen at the base of the spine and indicates that the spinal canal has been exposed. This is because the neural tube does not close properly to form the vertebrae. The severity of spina bifida varies from mild (such as a hairy patch) to severe paralysis. Neural tube defects occur in about 3 in every 1000 pregnancies in England and Wales. They are thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. The risk of having a child with spina bifida can be reduced by making sure that both partners take a daily supplement of 400 micrograms of folic acid (vitamin B9) before conception and throughout the first trimester of pregnancy. Folic acid is found in some breakfast cereals. However, taking extra folic acid supplements is recommended because it is difficult to get enough folic acid from food alone. It is important that women who are trying to conceive do not take higher than the recommended daily amount of folic acid (1mg or 1,200 micrograms). Taking too much folic acid could mask vitamin B12 deficiency, and this can lead to serious and irreversible nerve damage. A fatty acid which contains no double carbon-carbon bonds is a saturated fatty acid. All natural fats contain a mix of unsaturated and saturated fatty acids. Most naturally occurring fats are a mixture of both unsaturated and saturated fatty acids. The number of hydrogen atoms in a fatty acid chain determines whether it is saturated or unsaturated. In a saturated fatty acid there is one single bond between each pair of carbons. Therefore every carbon atom in the chain is attached to two other carbons and has two hydrogens attached to it. An unsaturated fatty acid has one or more double bonds in its chain. This means that some of the carbon atoms in the chain are not attached to a hydrogen atom. ### Arteriosclerosis and Atherosclerosis Arteriosclerosisis the process whereby the tunica media becomes thicker and the internal elastic lamina loses its elasticity. This causes the lumen to become narrower. Atherosclerosis occurs when LDLs react with LDL receptors on macrophages, allowing cholesterol to accumulate within the cell. This attracts more macrophages which then release collagenous fibres and cause foam cells to form. This is the first stage in plaque formation. Collagen synthesis is upregulated by PDGF, TNF-alpha and IL-1. Subendothelium tears can occur and allow collagen to be exposed to the blood. Macrophages will then ingest the collagen and this leads to further collagen production. Further tears can occur, leading to a cycle which eventually results in a fibrous cap forming over the atheroma. The atheroma is unstable and prone to rupture. Closure of the foramen ovale-This is the flap valve in the right atria that allows blood to bypass the lungs in foetuses as they are not using them. When the baby takes their first breath, oxygen is sent to the lungs and therefore the pressure in the pulmonary system drops (the pulmonary artery will have high pressure). The pressure difference causes the foramen ovale to shut, so blood no longer flows from the mother to the baby, but only from the baby to the mother. This prevents a potential flood of blood into the lungs. Closure of the umbilical arteries-These are closed very quickly after birth due to the lack of nutrient supply from the placenta. Closure of the umbilical vein occurs a few seconds later when the umbilical vein compresses and closes off at its inferior end. This happens because the placenta continues to remove nutrients from the foetus after birth. Closure of the ductus venosus-The ductus venosus shuts down within minutes of birth. This is due to the fact that the liver has now been perfused by the hepatic portal vein instead of the umbilical vein. Closure of the ductus arteriosus-Oxygenated blood travels through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. The pulmonary artery exerts a higher pressure than the descending aorta, which carries deoxygenated blood to the body. Therefore, there is high pressure in the lungs and low pressure in the descending aorta. This leads to closure of the ductus arteriosus. This mechanism is called the 'ventilatory shunt'. It is ventilation, rather than perfusion, that determines the closure of the ductus arteriosus. If the child is placed on a heart-lung machine, the ductus arteriosus may remain patent until perfusion returns to normal. This is a case of respiratory acidosis which has been compensated by metabolic alkalosis. The pH value is high indicating that the condition has been compensated.  PaO2 is normal or low in respiratory failure and is therefore not the primary cause of the alteration in acid base balance. The pH demonstrates that this is respiratory acidosis which can be worked out from the equation HCO3- x 0.42 + [PCO2] - 8 = pH. In this situation there will be increased ventilation as part of the compensation so the PaCO2 will be decreased (as it is here).  The degree of metabolic alkalosis can be worked out from the BE value which is greater than 2.
